column4: The section explicitly invokes this rain after despair: God sends relief-giving rain and spreads mercy when hope has failed, making the nurturing cloud an enacted form of divine care.
God drives clouds, joins them, then makes them a heap before rain emerges; this directly stages the source dictionary's cloud whose parts ride one above another.
Mercy-bearing winds lift a heavy cloud, which God drives to dead land so rain can bring every fruit; the whole cloud-water-growth movement is present.
A garden on elevated ground doubles its yield under heavy rain and still benefits from drizzle. This is the section's rain-fed growth scene; rabwa supplies no Rabb-root proof.
Mary's Lord receives her well, causes her to grow a beautiful growth, and repeatedly provides for her; human care and plant nurture meet exactly as the section proposes.
One ayah joins sheltering cloud, twelve water-springs struck from rock, known drinking places, and food provision, concentrating the section's cloud, flowing water, and nurture images.
Some rocks burst into rivers and others split so water comes out; this directly illuminates the source dictionary's nahr as water that cleaves earth.
Rain fills valleys according to their measure and the torrent bears passing foam; it gives the source's overflowing watercourse a Quranic scene of gathered flow, measure, and remainder.
The fertilizing winds are followed by water sent from heaven for people to drink, while God remains its true keeper; this realizes the source's moist wind as provision.
The section explicitly cites Mary and her son being given refuge on settled high ground with flowing water, joining shelter, stability, and provision without claiming a Rabb root for rabwa.
Paradise contains rivers of unspoiled water and milk whose taste never changes; nahr, abundant milk, and permanence converge in one scene.
The section explicitly joins rivers beneath lasting gardens with reciprocal pleasure between God and the servants, making flowing abundance and satisfaction one reward.
Like 98:8, this reward scene combines lasting gardens with rivers and the exact reciprocal relation: God is pleased with them and they with Him.
The first believers receive gardens with rivers and reciprocal divine-human pleasure, repeating the precise meeting of nahr and satisfaction highlighted by the section.
God strengthens the faithful, admits them to gardens with rivers, and is pleased with them as they are with Him; inner nurture, river, and mutual pleasure coincide.
The Lord makes earth and sky habitable, sends water down, and brings out fruits as provision; this is Rabb disclosed through the nurturing work behind the source's cloud-name.
Water revives the earth after death while winds turn and the cloud is held between sky and earth; the section's whole atmospheric ecology appears together.
Water from heaven produces every kind of growth, green shoots, grain, clustered dates, vines, olives, and pomegranates; cloud-water becomes differentiated nourishment.
Good land brings out vegetation by its Lord's permission, while bad land yields only scant growth; it states both Rabb-like nurture and the soil's boundary in receiving it.
Neighboring plots, vineyards, crops, and palms drink one water yet differ in fruit; the ayah sharpens how the same gathered water nurtures distinct growth.
Lightning brings fear and hope while God raises heavy clouds; this supplies the dense cloud itself and the expectant stance before its water falls.
The good tree gives fruit every season by its Lord's permission; it closely answers the source dictionary's summer-enduring plant and Rabb as sustaining nurture.
Water sent from heaven becomes both drink and vegetation in which livestock graze, linking abundant water, pasture, and provision.
The same water in 16:10 grows crops, olives, palms, grapes, and every fruit; this ayah supplies the differentiated growth completed by its rain-bearing neighbor.
God sends water from heaven and revives dead earth, a compact statement of the dry-ground and nurturing-water image.
God spreads earth, opens ways through it, sends water down, and produces diverse pairs of plants; prepared ground and measured growth form one act of care.
People eat and pasture their livestock from the plants of 20:53, turning the rain-grown landscape into shared nurture for human and herd.
The statement that every living thing was made from water articulates the life-giving premise made visible by the section's cloud and growing soil.
Human development from womb to maturity is set beside lifeless earth that stirs, swells, and grows after rain; personal nurture and plant nurture interpret each other.
Water descends and the earth becomes green, directly rendering the section's cloud passing over dry land as visible divine gentleness.
Water is sent down in due measure and lodged in the earth, with its removal remaining possible; gathered water is both precisely provided and vulnerable to withdrawal.
The lodged water of 23:18 raises palm-and-grape gardens with abundant fruit and food, completing the source's water-to-growth motion.
Winds arrive as good news before mercy, then pure water descends; this is the Quranic counterpart to the source dictionary's moist wind.
The pure water of 25:48 revives dead land and gives drink to livestock and people, extending rain from plant life into animal and human care.
God sends water and thereby grows gardens whose trees humans could not grow, making the distinction between receiving provision and causing growth explicit.
Even the question's opponents acknowledge that God sends water and revives dead earth; the nurturing act is presented as recognizable evidence.
Lightning is shown for fear and hope, rain descends, and earth revives after death; cloud-weather becomes an alternation of apprehension and promised growth.
The winds are glad tidings and a means of tasting mercy, seeking bounty, and becoming grateful; this makes the source's damp wind a bearer of نعمة in function.
God sends winds to raise clouds, spreads and fragments them, and rain emerges from within; the ayah closely stages the construction and release of a layered cloud.
Before that rain reaches them, people had been in despair; this gives the emotional threshold that the section explicitly associates with rain.
The commanded observer sees the effects of divine mercy in earth revived after death, completing the wind-cloud-despair sequence of 30:48-49.
Water from heaven causes every noble kind to grow from earth; the wording makes rain an answer to the section's Rabb-like cultivation.
Water is driven to barren land and brings crops eaten by livestock and people, reproducing dry ground, guided water, growth, and feeding in one scene.
Saba's two gardens are a sign and a provision to be eaten with gratitude; cultivated abundance is explicitly received as the Lord's good gift.
Winds raise clouds that are driven to a dead land, where the earth is revived; the source's moving cloud over dry soil is almost diagrammed.
Dead earth is revived and yields grain for food, making growth itself the sign of supplied life.
Palm-and-grape gardens receive springs made to gush within them; flowing water enters the cultivated ground rather than remaining merely beside it.
The fruit grown through the preceding springs becomes food, ending the revival sequence in nourishment and gratitude.
Rain is conducted into springs, then varied crops grow, wither, yellow, and become debris; it joins hidden watercourses to the exact boundary between sustained and passing growth.
Humbled, lifeless earth stirs and swells when water falls; the dry ground visibly receives the nurturing power attributed to the cloud.
Water descends from heaven in due measure and revives a dead land, directly joining measure, provision, and renewal.
Rain-provision revives earth after death in the same sign as the turning of the winds, uniting the section's wet wind and growing ground.
The believers are likened to a crop whose shoot strengthens, thickens, and stands firm; human formation is read through plant growth just as the section reads orphan-care through soil.
Blessed water descends and grows gardens and harvest grain, explicitly naming rain itself as a bearer of blessing.
Tall palms with layered clusters show the structured abundance produced by the blessed water of 50:9.
The rain-grown produce is provision for servants and revives a dead land, making nourishment the aim of the preceding cloud-water scene.
The hearer is made to look at what is sown, focusing the receiving ground and the human expectation of growth.
The question asks whether humans make the crop grow or God does; it isolates the nurturing agency that the source hears in Rabb.
The water people drink is placed before them as something received rather than self-produced.
The question asks whether people sent that water down from the rain-cloud or God did, directly locating provision in the cloud.
Forgiveness is followed by heaven sending abundant rain, so bestowed water appears as renewed favor rather than an automatic possession.
The rain of 71:11 is unfolded into wealth, children, gardens, and rivers; nurture multiplies across family, plant, and flowing-water forms.
God causes human beings to grow from earth as a growth, an exact Quranic meeting of personal nurture and plant vocabulary.
Pouring water descends from rain-laden clouds, giving the section's dense cloud its abundant release.
The pouring water brings out grain and vegetation, directly completing the rain-cloud action in 78:14.
Dense gardens are the culminating growth of the preceding rain, matching the source's cloud named for raising plants.
God brings earth's water and pasture out from it, joining hidden supply, emergence, and feeding ground.
The water and pasture are declared provision for people and livestock, stating the nurturing purpose of the preceding landscape.
Water is poured down abundantly, opening the most detailed Quranic sequence of water, cleft soil, growth, and food.
Earth is split open after the downpour; this directly parallels the source dictionary's explanation that a nahr cleaves the ground.
Grain is grown in the cleft, watered earth, beginning the sequence's edible yield.
Grapes and herbage emerge from the same watered ground, widening growth toward both human food and pasture.
Olives and palms add durable, fruit-bearing plants to the rain-fed sequence.
Dense gardens complete the transformation from poured water and split soil to sheltered abundance.
Fruit and pasture state the double yield of the garden scene for people and animals.
The entire water-growth sequence is named provision for people and their livestock, making nurture its explicit conclusion.
The sky characterized by returning rain supplies the recurring descent behind growth rather than a single accidental shower.
The earth characterized by cracking pairs with the returning sky, closely matching water's cleaving of ground in the source's nahr explanation.
The imperative to glorify the name of the Most High Lord begins a sequence that displays Rabb through creation, measure, guidance, and pasture.
God creates and makes fit, supplying the formative side of nurture before the pasture appears.
God measures and guides, presenting growth as directed and proportioned rather than merely abundant.
God brings out pasture after the command to glorify the Lord, directly joining Rabb and plant-raising in one compact passage.
The oath by the sun and its ضُحَاهَا gives the section's named duha branch its bright, unobscured celestial state.
God darkens the sky's night and brings out its ضُحَاهَا; the ayah places the bright state and night together as the two atmospheric poles read in 93:1-2.
The prayer remembers parents who رَبَّيَانِي, “raised me,” when small; this is the human nurturing action from which the section understands the name Rabb.
Cloud shades the vulnerable community while manna and quails feed them, making the cloud itself part of shelter and provision.
A struck stone releases twelve springs and each people knows its drinking place; hard ground opens into measured communal water.
Water sent from heaven brings fruit as provision, while rivers are subjected for human use; rain-grown food and nahr meet in one beneficent order.
Two gardens yield fully while a river is made to gush between them, directly joining fertile plants with an active watercourse.
At Mary's moment of isolation and grief, a stream is placed beneath her; running water becomes immediate refuge and reassurance.
Mary is directed to the palm and receives fresh dates beside the stream, completing sheltering water with nourishing fruit.
God makes earth a settled place and sets rivers through it; the watercourse is part of making land inhabitable.
Winds announce mercy before it arrives, paralleling the wet south-wind dictionary sense and the rain-bearing glad tidings elsewhere.
Earth is made to burst with springs and its water meets the water from heaven for a decreed matter, an extreme scene of abundant water gathering.
Two flowing springs animate the promised gardens, presenting water as the garden's continuing interior supply.
Every fruit occurs in pairs beside those springs, completing flowing water with sustained botanical abundance.
A second pair of gardens contains two gushing springs, repeating the association of garden shelter with active water.
Fruit, palms, and pomegranates are the yield surrounding those gushing springs.
The garden reward includes poured or continuously flowing water, an image of accessible abundance rather than water hidden beyond reach.
Abundant fruit accompanies that flowing water, linking supply to edible growth.
The fruit is neither cut off nor forbidden; its continuity illuminates the source dictionary's plants that do not fail in summer.
If water sinks beyond reach, no one can bring flowing water; the question precisely tests the source's well-reaching-water image against hidden withdrawal.
Remaining straight on the way is answered with abundant water, making overflowing supply a test-bearing divine gift.
The God-fearing are placed amid shade and springs, a concise pairing of refuge and accessible water.
The rewarded person is in a high garden, supplying the elevated refuge side of the section's cited Mary scene.
A flowing spring lies within that high garden, completing height and refuge with running water.
The promised garden has rivers beneath it and food and shade that endure; it joins nahr with the source's non-withering plant and persistent cover.
Livestock yield pure, palatable milk from within their bodies; this directly corresponds to the source dictionary's secondary sajw scene of a milk-abundant she-camel.
Livestock provide milk from their bellies along with many benefits and food, again giving Quranic content to the dictionary's abundant-milk animal.
A fertile, rivered orchard is struck by a fiery whirlwind and burns; this reverses the source's moist wind and nurturing water at the point of greatest need.
A freezing wind destroys the crop of people who wrong themselves; it is a precise opposite to the source dictionary's damp, life-bearing wind.
Rain makes earth's plants luxuriant and adorned, but destruction leaves them as though absent yesterday; the same growth scene exposes abundance's transience.
Earth swallows floodwater and sky withholds it until the water subsides; gathered abundance here belongs to judgment and must be contained, reversing nurturing rain.
Heavenly water mingles with earth's vegetation, which becomes dry fragments scattered by winds; it marks the boundary between rain-raised life and passing worldly display.
An abandoned well stands among ruined settlements; it is the stark reversal of the source dictionary's well that becomes abundant and reaches water.
Waves layered above waves with cloud overhead produce compounded darkness; the piled structure echoes the source's overlapping cloud, but here it obscures rather than nourishes.
Pharaoh claims نُرَبِّكَ, that he reared Moses as a child; the Rabb-root's nurturing sense is placed in a coercive speaker's self-serving claim.
Saba turns away, so the dam-flood replaces its two fruitful gardens with bitter, sparse growth; collected water crosses from gift into destructive reversal.
The people see an approaching cloud and call it rain-bearing, but it is the hastened punishment, a painful wind; expectation of nurture is explicitly overturned.
The wind from 46:24 destroys everything by its Lord's command, supplying that mistaken rain-cloud's actual effect rather than adding an independent cloud scene.
The wind sent against Aad is called barren or sterile, a lexical and functional opposite to the source's moist wind and the Quran's fertilizing winds.
Those who see a piece of sky falling dismiss it as a piled cloud; the exact heaped-cloud appearance becomes a figure of denied judgment rather than plant nurture.
Heaven's gates open with pouring water in the flood, supplying the descending half of the waters that meet in 54:12; abundance here executes judgment.
God could make the cloud-sent water bitter; the ayah marks drinkable water as contingent favor rather than an assured natural result.
Rain-produced growth delights cultivators, then withers, yellows, and becomes debris; it directly opposes the source dictionary's summer-enduring plant.
When water overflowed, humanity's line was carried in the Ark; abundant gathered water becomes both catastrophic boundary and a setting for preservation.
The pasture brought out in 87:4 is made dark stubble, setting divine growth beside its divinely governed ending and reversing the non-yellowing summer plant.
Gardens with rivers are set beside pleasure from God; although reciprocity is not stated here, the same reward passage connects nahr and divine approval.
Gardens, rivers, and good dwellings are followed by God's greater pleasure, extending the section's river-and-satisfaction meeting into sheltered reward.
The good word is compared to a firmly rooted tree with branches in heaven; 14:25 supplies its constant, Lord-permitted fruit, so the ayah contributes the stable organism.
After rain, fruit, and rivers in 14:32, the gifts are summarized as God's uncountable نعمة; the source's blessing word receives concrete water-and-growth content from its neighbor.
The corrupt word is an uprooted tree without stability, forming the explicit boundary opposite the enduring, Lord-nurtured tree of 14:24-25.
After the rain and crops of 16:10-11, God's نعمة is declared uncountable; the named blessing is thus concretized by water, pasture, and fruit.
Every moving creature is said to be created from water; this broadens the section's plant-centered water into animal life while retaining a concrete life-from-water claim.
Livestock provide benefits and drinks, plausibly including milk in context; this supports the source dictionary's milk-abundant animal, though the drink is not named here.
Lofty chambers with rivers beneath combine elevated shelter and flowing water, echoing the refuge scene without its agricultural detail.
A water-drawer lowers his bucket into a well and finds Joseph instead; the well's hidden depth yields an unforeseen human provision rather than merely water.
Fruit desired by the God-fearing grows within the shade-and-springs setting of 77:41, completing refuge and water with nourishment.
Hud joins seeking the Lord's forgiveness to abundant rain from heaven and increased strength, making water a renewed act of nurture after human return.
The faithful enter lasting gardens with rivers and deep shade; flowing water, enduring growth, and shelter meet in one reward scene.
A garden's water may sink so deeply that its owner cannot reach it, directly reversing the source dictionary's well dug until water is attained.
At Madyan's water Moses finds a community watering its herds and two women held back, making accessible water the center of vulnerability, animals, and social provision.
Moses waters the women's animals, withdraws into shade, and asks his Lord for good; supplied water, refuge, service, and acknowledged need converge.
Water sent from heaven brings fruits of differing colors, another direct formulation of cloud-water becoming varied plant provision.
The God-fearing are placed amid gardens and springs, closely pairing sheltering growth with continuing water.
The inhabitants are told to enter that garden-and-spring setting in peace and security, supplying the refuge quality of the preceding scene.
Gardens and springs are named among the provisions given to Aad, concretizing divine support as cultivated growth and accessible water.
Salih asks whether his people expect to remain secure in their present setting; the following gardens and springs define the refuge whose permanence they presume.
Gardens and springs supply the watered landscape in which Thamud feels secure.
Crops and palms with tender fruit complete the preceding springs-and-gardens scene as edible growth.
Within Abraham's description of the Lord of all worlds, God is the one who feeds him and gives him drink; Rabb is disclosed through direct nurture.
God withholds unlimited provision lest people transgress and sends it in the measure He wills; this gives the rain after despair in 42:28 its governing principle of fitted supply.
Immediately after the rain-revival sequence, a sent wind can leave the growth yellow; it sharply reverses both the moist wind and the non-yellowing summer plant in the source.
Water sent from heaven at Badr purifies the believers, removes defilement, strengthens hearts, and steadies feet; rain nurtures vulnerable people rather than soil here.
God splits grain and date-stone and brings living from dead, an indirect plant-side parallel to water cleaving ground and awakening growth.
Joseph is deliberately hidden in the well's unseen depth so a caravan may recover him; 12:19 then turns the expected search for water into discovery of a protected child.
The command to look at earth's many noble kinds of growth supports the section's reading of cultivated vegetation as a perceptible divine sign.
The God-fearing occupy a secure station; the next ayah identifies its garden-and-spring setting, so this row contributes stable refuge.
Gardens and springs furnish the water and growth within the secure station named in 44:51.
Extended shade stands immediately beside poured water and abundant, uninterrupted fruit, adding persistent shelter to that water-and-growth passage.
Noah commands his people to seek their Lord's forgiveness; this ayah supplies the penitential stance to which abundant rain, gardens, and rivers answer in 71:11-12.
Cloud canopies accompany the awaited coming of divine judgment and angels; the familiar cloud-object here signals final decision rather than plant nurture.
The river tests Saul's troops through a strict boundary on drinking, turning abundant flowing water into a measure of restraint and obedience.
The gushing oven marks the flood's onset and the command to board pairs; overflowing water becomes a boundary of judgment and rescue rather than agricultural nurture.
The opponents demand that the Prophet make a spring gush from earth before they will believe, converting the hidden-water scene into a coercive test of revelation.
They further demand a palm-and-grape garden with rivers explosively coursing through it, turning water-grown abundance into a skeptical condition for faith.
Noah is told to load the Ark when the oven gushes; abundant emerging water becomes the onset of judgment while the vessel preserves selected life.
The sky splits open with cloud and descending angels, giving cloud an eschatological role wholly different from its nurturing rain function.
Fresh, sweet water and salty, bitter water meet yet remain divided by a barrier; the boundary clarifies that not every abundance of water is equally fit to nourish.
One sea is fresh and pleasant to drink while the other is salty, yet both yield food and support ships; water's fitness for drinking has a precise boundary without ending provision.
Pharaoh points to rivers flowing beneath him as evidence of his kingship, appropriating nahr as a sign of human domination rather than the Lord's nurture.
The garden owners are tested when they resolve to harvest in the morning; cultivated provision becomes a moral trial over who may receive its fruit.
After the nocturnal visitation, the garden becomes like a reaped or darkened field, another sharp reversal from flourishing provision to withdrawn growth.
